nodes.question: What was the purpose of the research team's meeting after the analysis?
nodes.answer: The research team met to discuss the identified themes and resolve any differences in the themes that were identified.
nodes.paragraph: Our inclusion criteria were: HIA practitioners, academics, educators or commissioners or other relevant HIA experience (self-identified). The sur - vey asked the following: the participant S current role, country currently based in, background in and experi - ence of HIA, their views on important areas of research for HIA, the priority research questions and how to build and support HIA research, what they think the research needs are and how we could support the development of HIA research over the next 10 years. The closed questions were descriptively analysed. Two members of the team (FH and MD) separately carried out thematic analysis of the open questions to identify key themes in relation to the questions; What do you think the most important areas of research needed in the field of HIA in the next ten years? What do you think the most important unresolved research questions in HIA are? How can we build and support HIA research? What are important factors/ next steps/ approaches that we should be considering? The research team met to discuss these and resolve any difference in themes identified.

nodes.question: What is essential for analyzing disagreements according to the text?
nodes.answer: Investigating the underlying conflicting worldviews is essential for analyzing disagreements.
nodes.paragraph: Conflicts arise not only from clashing values and power imbalances (GI ck, 1994) but also from divergent perceptions (Hoogstra-Klein et al., 2012; Pokorny & Schanz, 2003). What is perceived as a problem, which solution becomes preferred by whom, and who bears the responsibility for both problems and solutions are central. Analyzing dis- agreements by investigating underlying conflicting worldviews is instrumental (Pokorny & Schanz, 2003). Several theoretical approaches or frameworks have been employed to study EU forest policy and its actors, such as discourse analysis/discursive agency (e.g., Leipold et al., 2016), Advocacy Coalition Framework (ACF), Shifting Coalitions Theory (SCT) (e.g. Sotirov et al., 2021), policy integration theories (e.g., P lzl et al., 2018), Multi-Level Governance (MLG) (e.g., P Izl et al., 2014), and Institutional Anal- ysis and Development (IAD) Framework (e.g., de Koning & Cleaver, 2012). According to Mamadouh (1999b), it is important to understand political institutions and actions in a cultural context, as political activities are directed by interpretations and prefer - ences, not by bare facts and interests.

nodes.question: How does Antonio Gramsci integrate critical analysis into his work?
nodes.answer: Antonio Gramsci integrates critical analysis into his examination of common sense, suggesting it is essential for developing what he calls good sense.
nodes.paragraph: Following this tradition, theorist and activist Clara Zet- kin argued in relation to social equity and the women S movement in the early twentieth century that a critical, historical attitude to those problems must lead to a ruth- less examination of society, to a disclosure of its real nature (Zetkin 1934). Activist, political leader, and social theorist Antonio Gramsci S critical analysis is integrated into his well-known examination of common sense or the generally held assumptions of a given society and the possibility for developing what he called good sense (Gramsci 1971). In doing so, Gramsci suggests that criti- cal analysis is necessarily based in a scientific form of thought. Transcending common sense cannot but pre- sent itself at the outset in a polemical and critical guise, as superseding the existing mode of thinking and exist- ing concrete thought it must be a criticism of common sense (Gramsci 1971, p. 330). The ruthlessness of the critical approach we elaborate for sustainability science is based on this well-established critical tradition. It is intended as a sharp and robust effort to illuminate essential questions and problems of our time and to arrive at sound evidence-based conclusions.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Governance|Peace, justice and strong institutions|Peacebuilding efforts|Conflict analysis workshops_qna_006
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What is the main focus of the analysis described in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The main focus of the analysis is on critically examining the deep-seated assumptions and social conditions underlying scientific inquiry and addressing sustainability problems, irrespective of ideological confrontations or powerful actors in various realms.
nodes.paragraph: It is an analysis based in the deep-seated interrogation that lies at the heart of scientific inquiry and the manner to address sustainability problems, irrespective of the ideological con - frontations or the powerful actors it challenges, whether they be in the political, economic, or scientific realms. A grounding aspect of this approach is its scrutinty of taken-for-granted social conditions and assumptions. A criti- cal analysis is one that judiciously examines the prevailing social order and takes seriously the possibility and even the necessity for alternatives (Marcuse 2013). As such, it is indispensable for what contemporary sustainability science often refers to as sustainability transitions or transformations (e.g., Alonso-Adame et al. 2024; Davelaar 2021; Sahle et al. 2024a, b). Critical sustainability science draws fundamentally on the logic of science, even though it can and often does interrogate the institution of science (York 2021; York and Clark 2010). Importantly, in opposition to other cul- turally based critical approaches including for example post-structuralist, -modernist, -humanist, -Marxist criti- cal sustainability science is erected on a realist/materialist and dialectical footing.

nodes.question: What tensions exist within the different framings of co-production?
nodes.answer: There are tensions between analytical and instrumental framings, where analytical modes critique knowledge and power relationships, while instrumental modes seek to build and navigate these relationships.
nodes.paragraph: Berkes, 2009 ) 2) modes of critical analyses for understanding how knowledge and societal values and goals are created inter-dependently (e.g. Jasanoff, 2004 ) and, 3) means of coordinating public, private and third sector action to create societal outcomes (e.g. Ostrom and Ostrom, 1977 ). Its applica- tion across different sectors and disciplines has generated diverse meanings (Bandola-Gill et al. 2021 ) and purposes (Chambers et al. 2021 ). Here we refer to co-production, after Wyborn et al. (2019 p. 320) as the processes that iteratively bring together diverse groups and their ways of knowing and acting to create newknowledge and practices to transform societal outcomes This de nition and emerging tradition link the three strands of co-production described above into a form of praxis that is, ideally, re exive and critical, engaged and empathetic, and oriented by clear and shared societal goals. Across these distinct lineages of co-production there has been tensions between analytical and instrumental framings of co-production. On one hand, analytical and descriptive modes of co- production seek to critique the relationships between knowledge and power, while instrumental and normative framings look to build and navigate the relationships between knowledge and power (Perry, 2022 , Wyborn, 2015 , L vbrand, 2011 ).

nodes.question: What is the purpose of the developed diagnostic approach mentioned in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The diagnostic approach aims to provide an operationalising framework and workshop activities to help research teams critically reflect on co-production foundational aspects.
nodes.paragraph: Fit here is used in a Dar- winian sense of being well-suited to the setting. Outcome- oriented is a reminder, from the preparatory stage, of the need to generate meaningful outcomes through the co-production endeavours (i.e. that hold relevancy, legitimacy and saliency) for the parties involved, to build/maintain trust in the partner- ship and, particularly for publicly funded research organisations, with the public. We use the term diagnose in the sense of dis- tinguishing, discerning, or distinctively characterising the research context, the research team S composition and cap- abilities and potential strategic approaches. To progress such work, we developed a diagnostic approach, including an oper- ationalising framework and workshop activities to support research teams to critically re ect on foundational aspects of co- production for their research. Given the multiple possible options for doing co-production and uncertainties that exist prior to engaging with stakeholders, we intend this framework as a heuristic device to be adaptively applied with and by teams (McKeown et al. 2022 ). Secondly, in trialling and testing the heuristic and workshop series process (hereafter approach ), we asked in what ways (in the immediate-short term) did the approach assist research teams with re exive practice, in planning t-for-purpose, outcome- oriented co-production within their research?

nodes.id: Subtopic:Governance|Peace, justice and strong institutions|Peacebuilding efforts|Conflict analysis workshops_qna_009
nodes.label: Methodology
nodes.question: What methodology is employed in this research?
nodes.answer: The research employs the problematisation approach, which includes defining a domain of investigation, evaluating assumptions, developing alternative perspectives, conducting qualitative interviews, and assessing alternative assumptions, alongside a systematic literature review and semi-structured interviews with experts.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Purpose This research aims to develop a critical understanding of the employment of digital technologies (DTs) for LCA studies, outlining both the opportunities and challenges associated with circular strategies. Two research questions are thus addressed: (1) What circular loops and aspects are addressed when digital technologies are integrated in the development of a Life Cycle Inventory? (2) Which trade-offs are revealed in the integration of digital technologies in Life Cycle Inventory development addressing circularity along a life cycle? Methods This study is based on the problematisation approach, which critically examines existing assumptions in the LCA literature, structured into six principles: defining a domain of investigation, articulating and evaluating assumptions, develop- ing alternative perspectives, involving the audience through qualitative interviews, and assessing the alternative assumptions. A systematic literature review (SLR) and semi-structured interviews with experts were conducted to explore these issues and suggest future research directions. Results and discussion It emerges that the DTs are mainly integrated in the Life Cycle Inventory phase capturing closing and narrowing loops, whereas a limited number of cases investigate slowing loops with different aspects investigated.
